headings.title: Introduction and Chain of Survival in ACLS
headings.content: Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support (ACLS) builds upon basic life support skills to provide urgent, coordinated interventions for patients experiencing life-threatening cardiovascular emergencies, such as cardiac arrest, stroke, and acute arrhythmias. At the heart of ACLS practice is the AHA Chain of Survival, a systematic sequence of events designed to maximize the probability of patient survival and neurological recovery. For out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, the chain includes early recognition and prevention, immediate high-quality CPR, rapid defibrillation, advanced resuscitation by emergency medical services, post-cardiac arrest care, and recovery. In the in-hospital setting, the chain places a heavy emphasis on early surveillance, prevention, and rapid response team activation to prevent arrests before they happen. Nigerian nursing students must understand that every link in this chain is interdependent. A failure in early recognition or a delay in initiating high-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation significantly reduces the patient's overall chances of survival, regardless of how advanced the subsequent hospital care might be. As future nursing leaders in various clinical settings across Nigeria, nurses play a pivotal role in initiating the chain by recognizing subtle patient deteriorations, calling for help immediately, and beginning basic life support measures while awaiting the multidisciplinary resuscitation team. Mastering these foundational concepts ensures a smooth transition from basic life-saving measures to advanced clinical interventions during critical emergencies.

headings.title: Basic Life Support (BLS) Foundation and High-Quality CPR
headings.content: High-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) serves as the absolute bedrock of both Basic Life Support (BLS) and Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support (ACLS). Without effective chest compressions and ventilation, advanced pharmacological and electrical interventions have a drastically reduced chance of restoring a perfusing cardiac rhythm. For healthcare providers, high-quality CPR entails pushing hard and fast: compressing the adult chest at a depth of at least 2 inches (5 cm) but not greater than 2.4 inches (6 cm), at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute. Allowing complete chest recoil after each compression is crucial because it allows the heart chambers to refill with blood between strokes. Furthermore, minimizing interruptions in chest compressions is vital; pauses should ideally be kept under 10 seconds, such as during rhythm checks or advanced airway placement. Ventilation must also be carefully managed to avoid hyperventilation, which increases intrathoracic pressure and decreases venous return to the heart. When an advanced airway is not yet in place, a compression-to-ventilation ratio of 30:2 is maintained for adults. Nursing students must practice these parameters rigorously on simulation manikins, as muscular fatigue can rapidly compromise compression depth and rate during a real resuscitation attempt. Recognizing and correcting poor CPR technique immediately is a core competency expected of professional nurses in any emergency scenario.

headings.title: Cardiac Arrest Algorithms: Shockable vs. Non-Shockable Rhythms
headings.content: Cardiac arrest management relies heavily on the rapid identification of underlying cardiac rhythms via a monitor or defibrillator, dividing them into shockable and non-shockable categories. The two shockable rhythms are Ventricular Fibrillation (VF) and pulseless Ventricular Tachycardia (pVT). When these are identified, immediate defibrillation is indicated, followed by the resumption of high-quality CPR and the administration of emergency medications like epinephrine and amiodarone. Conversely, the non-shockable rhythms include Asystole and Pulseless Electrical Activity (PEA). For these rhythms, immediate defibrillation is contraindicated; instead, the priority is uninterrupted high-quality CPR, rapid identification and treatment of reversible causes (the H's and T's), and prompt administration of epinephrine every 3 to 5 minutes. Reversible causes such as hypovolemia, hypoxia, hydrogen ion acidosis, hypokalemia or hyperkalemia, hypothermia, tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, toxins, and thrombosis (pulmonary or coronary) must be systematically investigated and treated by the healthcare team. Nursing students must be proficient in reading rhythm strips and understanding that rushing to shock a non-shockable rhythm wastes critical time, whereas delaying a shock for VF/pVT drastically worsens patient outcomes. Effective team communication during rhythm analysis ensures that compressions are paused only when strictly necessary for rhythm checks and shock delivery.

headings.title: Advanced Airway Management and Ventilation Strategies
headings.content: Advanced airway management is a critical component of ACLS, aimed at securing an open airway, ensuring effective oxygenation and ventilation, and protecting the lungs from aspiration. Options range from basic adjuncts like oropharyngeal and nasopharyngeal airways to supraglottic airway devices (such as the laryngeal mask airway) and endotracheal intubation. Endotracheal intubation provides the most definitive airway control, but it requires specialized training and can cause interruptions in chest compressions if not performed efficiently. Once an advanced airway is successfully placed and confirmed (using physical assessment and waveform capnography), CPR mechanics change: compressions are delivered continuously at a rate of 100 to 120 per minute without pauses, and ventilations are delivered at a rate of 1 breath every 6 seconds (10 breaths per minute). Waveform capnography, which measures end-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO2), is considered the gold standard for confirming proper endotracheal tube placement and monitoring the ongoing quality of CPR. A sudden increase in EtCO2 can also serve as an early indicator of the return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Nurses assisting with airway management must prepare equipment beforehand, assist with suctioning, monitor oxygen saturation, and continuously observe patient color and chest rise to ensure the airway remains secure and patent throughout the resuscitation process.

headings.title: Pharmacological Agents and Emergency Vascular Access
headings.content: Pharmacological interventions during ACLS are designed to optimize coronary and cerebral perfusion, restore a normal cardiac rhythm, and manage post-arrest complications. Epinephrine remains the primary vasopressor used in cardiac arrest, administered at a dose of 1 mg IV/IO every 3 to 5 minutes, working primarily through alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction to increase aortic diastolic pressure and coronary blood flow. For refractory ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia, antiarrhythmic agents like amiodarone (first dose 300 mg, second dose 150 mg) or lidocaine may be administered. Establishing reliable emergency vascular access is imperative for drug delivery. Peripheral IV lines are quick to establish but require a 20 mL fluid bolus and extremity elevation to facilitate drug transit to the central circulation. If peripheral access fails or is unattainable during an emergency, intraosseous (IO) access serves as a rapid, safe, and effective alternative route in both adult and pediatric patients, allowing medications and fluids to enter the systemic circulation via the bone marrow. Central venous catheterization is another option, though it is often more time-consuming and carries risks such as pneumothorax. Nurses must be expert in calculating drug dosages rapidly, flushing lines correctly, and identifying suitable anatomical landmarks for IO insertion, such as the proximal tibia or humeral head.

headings.title: Management of Symptomatic Bradycardia and Tachycardia
headings.content: Managing abnormal heart rates requires quick assessment to determine if the patient is stable or unstable. Symptomatic bradycardia (heart rate less than 60 beats per minute with signs of poor perfusion such as hypotension, altered mental status, or signs of shock) is managed first with atropine at a dose of 1 mg IV, which can be repeated every 3 to 5 minutes up to a total dose of 3 mg. If atropine is ineffective, second-line interventions include transcutaneous pacing, an infusion of dopamine, or an epinephrine infusion. Conversely, tachycardia with a pulse is evaluated based on whether the patient is stable or unstable. Unstable tachycardia—manifesting with severe chest pain, shortness of breath, acute heart failure, hypotension, or signs of shock—demands immediate synchronized cardioversion to restore a normal rhythm. Stable tachycardia allows time for diagnostic evaluation, 12-lead ECG interpretation, and specific interventions such as vagal maneuvers or adenosine administration for regular narrow-complex tachycardias. Nigerian nursing students must recognize that instability is the critical trigger for immediate electrical intervention (cardioversion or pacing). Nurses must closely monitor vital signs, prepare emergency equipment, and provide clear reassurance and sedation when appropriate prior to performing synchronized electrical therapies.

headings.title: Post-Cardiac Arrest Care and Targeted Temperature Management
headings.content: Achieving Return of Spontaneous Circulation (ROSC) is a major milestone, but post-cardiac arrest care is crucial to reduce mortality and prevent neurological damage. Post-arrest management focuses on optimizing ventilation and oxygenation, maintaining adequate blood pressure and perfusion, and identifying and treating the precipitating cause of the arrest. Hypoxia and severe hypotension must be aggressively avoided, as secondary brain injury often occurs in the hours following resuscitation. For patients who remain comatose (unresponsive to verbal commands) after ROSC, Targeted Temperature Management (TTM) is strongly recommended. TTM involves actively cooling the patient to a constant core temperature between 32°C and 36°C for at least 24 hours to reduce metabolic demand, limit ischemic-reperfusion injury, and improve overall neurological outcomes. Nursing care during TTM requires meticulous monitoring of core temperature using esophageal, bladder, or tympanic probes, careful titration of sedatives and paralytic agents to prevent shivering, and vigilant assessment for complications such as arrhythmias, coagulopathies, hyperglycemia, and electrolyte imbalances. As nurses managing these vulnerable patients in intensive care units, careful monitoring ensures that the therapeutic window of cooling is maintained safely until gradual, controlled rewarming is initiated.

headings.title: Team Dynamics and Leadership in Resuscitation
headings.content: Advanced resuscitation is a complex multidisciplinary effort that requires exceptional teamwork, clear communication, and defined leadership to be successful. High-performance resuscitation teams utilize closed-loop communication—where orders are repeated back and acknowledged—to eliminate ambiguity and ensure tasks are executed safely. Team roles, such as the compressor, airway manager, defibrillator operator, and recorder/timekeeper, must be clearly assigned before or immediately at the start of an emergency. The team leader oversees the overall resuscitation strategy, monitors CPR quality, encourages performance, and plans ahead for interventions while remaining situationally aware. Constructive intervention is also encouraged, meaning any team member can and should speak up if they notice an error, such as inadequate compression depth or an overdue epinephrine dose, regardless of hierarchy. For nursing students in Nigeria, mastering these non-technical skills is just as important as mastering pharmacology or ECG interpretation. Cultivating a culture of mutual respect, clear role clarity, and psychological safety ensures that the resuscitation team functions as a cohesive unit, ultimately translating into higher survival rates and better patient outcomes in emergency departments and intensive care units.
